result.markdown: --- title: "DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics" subtitle: "Lecture 8: Logical Vectors" author: "Agassi Iu" institute: "Wilfrid Laurier University" date: "October 20, 2026" format: live-revealjs: resources: - data/sleep_survey_v2.csv theme: sky slide-number: true transition: slide incremental: true embed-resources: true # Embeds figures and libraries into a single portable HTML file filters: - live webr: packages: - ggplot2 - dplyr - tidyr - tibble - readr - stringr - forcats - purrr - scales execute: echo: true warning: false # Hides warnings and package loading messages message: false fig-width: 7 fig-height: 4 fig-align: center --- ::: {.cell} ::: # The question ## Do students who sleep less get lower grades, and does it depend on their program? {.center} - We have a survey of **1,000 students** - Today we answer this question, and learn Chapter 12 (logical vectors) *along the way* ::: {.notes} ~5 min for this whole opening block. Resist explaining any code yet: the point is to show the answer first. ::: ::: {.cell context='setup'} ::: ::: {.cell autorun='true'} ```{webr} #| include: false #| autorun: true library(dplyr) library(tibble) library(ggplot2) library(tidyverse) library(readr) survey <- read.csv("data/sleep_survey_v2.csv", fileEncoding = "WINDOWS-1252") ``` ::: ## Answer ::: {.cell context='output' autorun='true'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-8_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Answer: split by program ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-8_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## So how did we get here? Everything on the last two slides came from **one pipeline**: ```r sleep_summary <- survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program, sleep_group) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade), pct_passing = mean(avg_grade >= 60), any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ## The plan for today {.smaller} We rebuild the pipeline one action at a time. Each action needs a different part of Chapter 12: | Step | Action | Chapter 12 tools we need | |------|------|--------------------------| | 1 | `mutate()` | comparisons (`<`, `==`), `if_else()`, `case_when()` | | 2 | `filter()` | missing values, `is.na()`, `&`, |, `!`, `%in%` | | 3 | `group_by()` + `summarize()` | `sum()`, `mean()`, `any()`, `all()` | ::: {.callout-tip title="Not everything fits in this 80-minute lecture"} In future, I will leave some of the undiscussed functions or tools in an *appendix table* at the end of the slide deck. Each row will say what the tool does and which section of the chapter to read. You should definitely take a look at the text for more details. ::: ## Meet the data ::: {.cell} ```{webr} glimpse(survey) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note title="About this data"} - This is a **simulated** survey for teaching this class. Don't take the results seriously. - A blank cell means the student left the question unanswered. R reads it as `NA` - You will see those blanks cause trouble in a few minutes ::: ## What is a logical vector? ::: {.callout-note title="Definition"} A **logical vector** is the simplest kind of vector: every element is exactly one of three values. - `TRUE` - `FALSE` - `NA` (missing) ::: - Raw data rarely arrives as logical vectors - But you will create and use them in almost every analysis # Step 1: mutate() ## Where we are in the pipeline ```{.r code-line-numbers="2-8"} sleep_summary <- survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program, sleep_group) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade), pct_passing = mean(avg_grade >= 60), any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50), .groups = "drop" ) ``` **Goal:** turn `sleep_hours` (a number) into `sleep_group` (a label). ## The `mutate()` Function ::: {.callout-note title="Purpose"} Adds new columns or modifies existing ones in a data frame. It operates column-wise and preserves the total number of rows. ::: ```r # Example: Create new columns for weekly sleep and high-sleep status survey |> mutate( sleep_hours_week = sleep_hours * 7, high_sleep = sleep_hours > 7.5 ) ``` ## Creating logical vectors {.smaller} The comparison operators are: | Operator | Meaning | |---|---| | `<` | less than | | `<=` | less than or equal to | | `>` | greater than | | `>=` | greater than or equal to | | `==` | equal exactly to | | `!=` | not equal to | Each one compares two values and returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`. ## Who sleeps less than 6 hours? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate(short_sleep = sleep_hours < 6, .keep = "used") ``` ::: - `short_sleep` is a **logical column** - We can store it with `mutate()`, or use the same test directly inside `filter()` ## Choosing which columns survive {.smaller} `mutate()` has a `.keep` argument that controls which columns appear in the result. | `.keep =` | Columns returned | |-----------|------------------| | `"all"` (default) | All original columns plus the new ones | | `"used"` | Only the columns used to build the new ones, plus the new ones | | `"unused"` | Original columns you did not use, plus the new ones | | `"none"` | Only the new columns (plus any grouping variables) | ::: {.callout-tip title="Why we use it today"} `.keep = "used"` shows each input column next to the logical column it produced, so you can check the result by eye. It does not change the logic. ::: ## How many `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `NA`? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate(short_sleep = sleep_hours < 6) |> count(short_sleep) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-important title="A blank is not FALSE"} Students who left `sleep_hours` blank get `NA`, not `FALSE`. *R* does not know whether they slept less than 6 hours. - We deal with these rows in Step 2. ::: ## Comparing text `has_early_class` is stored as text (`"Yes"` / `"No"`). Comparisons work on text too: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate(early = has_early_class == "Yes", .keep = "used") |> count(has_early_class, early) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Spelling and capitals matter"} `"Yes"`, `"yes"`, and `"YES"` are three different values to R. Check how your data is spelled before you compare it. ::: ## Assigning labels using Logicals `if_else(condition, true, false)` picks one value when the condition is `TRUE` and another when it is `FALSE`. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_label = if_else(sleep_hours < 6, "Short", "Not short"), .keep = "used" ) |> count(sleep_label) ``` ::: - Two groups: fine - A blank `sleep_hours` stays `NA` ## What if we want three groups? We could nest one `if_else()` inside another: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = if_else( sleep_hours < 6, "Short", if_else(sleep_hours <= 7.5, "Normal", "Long") ), .keep = "used" ) |> count(sleep_group) ``` ::: - It works, but it is already hard to read - Every extra group adds another layer - Time for `case_when()` ## `case_when()` - Inspired by SQL's `CASE` statement - Uses a special syntax unlike anything else in the tidyverse: pairs of `condition ~ output` - `condition` must be a logical vector; when it is `TRUE`, `output` is used ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ), .keep = "used" ) ``` ::: ## Check your groups ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> count(sleep_group) ``` ::: - Where did the `NA` row come from? - No condition matched the blank `sleep_hours`, so `case_when()` gave `NA` ## Why "Normal" has no lower bound ::: {.callout-important title="Only the first match is used"} If several conditions are `TRUE` for one student, `case_when()` uses the **first** one. ::: - A student with `sleep_hours = 5` is `< 6` **and** `<= 7.5` - The `"Short"` line comes first, so it wins - That is why `"Normal"` does not need to say `sleep_hours >= 6` ## What if we swap the order? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> count(sleep_group) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Overlapping conditions"} There is no `"Short"` row any more. Every short sleeper matched `<= 7.5` first. Be careful with complex `case_when()` statements, especially when you mix `<` and `>`. ::: ## `.default` is a catch-all, and a trap ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", .default = "Long" ) ) |> count(sleep_group) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Where did the NA row go?"} `.default` also catches the blank rows. They are now labelled `"Long"`, which is wrong. We wrote `sleep_hours > 7.5` explicitly so blank rows stay `NA`. ::: ## Exercise 1 ::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"} Use `case_when()` to create a `grade_band` column from `avg_grade`: - `"Fail"`: below 50 - `"Pass"`: 50 to 69 - `"Good"`: 70 to 84 - `"Excellent"`: 85 and above Then use `count()` to see how many students are in each band. What happens to students with a blank `avg_grade`? ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_bands'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_bands survey |> mutate( grade_band = case_when( ) ) |> count(grade_band) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_bands' solution='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_bands #| solution: true survey |> mutate( grade_band = case_when( avg_grade < 50 ~ "Fail", avg_grade < 70 ~ "Pass", avg_grade < 85 ~ "Good", avg_grade >= 85 ~ "Excellent" ) ) |> count(grade_band) # The blank avg_grade rows show up as NA: no condition matched them. ``` ::: # Step 2: filter() ::: {.notes} ~20 min for this section including Exercise 2. The `== NA` failure and the `| 5` failure are the two "break it live" moments. ::: ## Where we are in the pipeline ```{.r code-line-numbers="9"} sleep_summary <- survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program, sleep_group) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade), pct_passing = mean(avg_grade >= 60), any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50), .groups = "drop" ) ``` **Goal:** remove the students with blank answers. This one line needs the most Chapter 12 ideas. ## `filter()` keeps `TRUE` rows ::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"} `filter()` keeps rows where the condition is `TRUE`. It drops rows where the condition is `FALSE` **or `NA`**. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(sleep_hours < 6) ``` ::: - Students with a blank `sleep_hours` are silently gone - Is that what we wanted? ## Missing values are "contagious" - `NA` stands for the *unknown* - Almost any operation involving an unknown value gives an unknown result ::: {.cell} ```{webr} NA > 5 10 == NA ``` ::: ## The most confusing case: `NA == NA` ::: {.cell} ```{webr} NA == NA ``` ::: Easier to see with some context: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} # We don't know how old Mary is age_mary <- NA # We don't know how old John is age_john <- NA # Are Mary and John the same age? age_mary == age_john # We don't know! ``` ::: ## Let's find the blank rows The obvious attempt: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(sleep_hours == NA) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Zero rows. Why?"} - `sleep_hours == NA` returns `NA` for **every** row - `filter()` drops rows where the condition is `NA` - So nothing is left ::: ## The fix: `is.na()` ::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"} Never test for missing values with `== NA`. Use `is.na()`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(is.na(sleep_hours)) ``` ::: `is.na(x)` works on any type of vector. It returns `TRUE` for missing values and `FALSE` for everything else. ## Keeping the complete rows Put `!` in front to flip `TRUE` and `FALSE`: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(!is.na(sleep_hours)) ``` ::: - `!is.na(x)` reads as "x is **not** missing" - This is the first half of our pipeline's `filter()` line ## Combining logical vectors Once you have several logical vectors, combine them with Boolean algebra: | Operator | Meaning | |----------|---------| | `&` | and | | | | or | | `!` | not | ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(program == "Arts" & sleep_hours < 6) ``` ::: - In `filter()`, a comma means the same as `&`: `filter(a, b)` is `filter(a & b)` - That is why our pipeline has `filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade))` ## Venn diagrams ![Common Boolean operations. `x` is the left circle, `y` is the right circle, and the shaded region shows what each operator selects. Figure from R for Data Science (2e), Fig. 12.1.](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/diagrams/transform.png){fig-alt="Seven Venn diagrams, one per logical operator: x & !y, x & y, !x & y, x, xor(x, y), y, and x | y." width="85%"} ## Missing values in Boolean algebra The rules look inconsistent at first: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} df <- tibble(x = c(TRUE, FALSE, NA)) df |> mutate( and = x & NA, or = x | NA, not = x != NA, check = is.na(x) ) ``` ::: ## Making sense of the `NA` rules Remember: an `NA` in a logical vector means "could be `TRUE` or `FALSE`". ::: {.callout-note title="Or (`|`): only one side needs to be `TRUE`"} - `TRUE | TRUE` and `FALSE | TRUE` are both `TRUE` - So `NA | TRUE` must be `TRUE`: whichever way the `NA` resolves, the result is `TRUE` - But `NA | FALSE` is `NA`: it depends on what the `NA` really is ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="And (`&`): both sides must be `TRUE`"} - `NA & TRUE` is `NA`: it depends on the `NA` - `NA & FALSE` is `FALSE`: at least one side is `FALSE` no matter what ::: ## R does not work like English ::: {.callout-warning title="A tempting mistake"} Suppose we want the high-stress students: stress level 4 **or** 5. In English that is easy to say... ::: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(stress_level == 4 | 5) |> select(stress_level) ``` ::: It does not give an error, but it does not work either. Every row came back. Why? ## What went wrong? 1. R first evaluates `stress_level == 4`, producing a logical vector (call it `four`) 2. Then it computes `four | 5` 3. With a logical operator, any number other than 0 is converted to `TRUE` 4. So this becomes `four | TRUE`, which is **always** `TRUE` 5. Every row is selected ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( four = stress_level == 4, final = four | 5, .keep = "used" ) ``` ::: ## The same mistake with text ::: {.cell} ```{webr} #| error: true survey |> filter(program == "Arts" | "Business") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Loud errors are the friendly ones"} With numbers, the mistake is **silent** and gives wrong results. With text, *R* basically stops and complains. Either way, *R* does not read English the way we do, so you should write the full comparison on both sides. ::: ## The correct version ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(stress_level == 4 | stress_level == 5) |> select(stress_level) ``` ::: That gets long. There is a shortcut. ## `%in%` `x %in% y` returns a logical vector the same length as `x`. It is `TRUE` whenever a value of `x` appears anywhere in `y`. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} 1:12 %in% c(1, 5, 11) ``` ::: An easy way to dodge the `==` / `|` ordering problem: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business")) ``` ::: ## `%in%` and missing values ::: {.callout-caution title="Different NA rules"} `%in%` follows different `NA` rules from `==`: `NA %in% NA` is `TRUE`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} c(1, 2, NA) == NA c(1, 2, NA) %in% NA ``` ::: ## Back to the pipeline By now we have removed the missing data under the columns with categorical variable with `sleep_hours` (i.e. `sleep_group`), and `avg_grade`. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> count(sleep_group) ``` ::: - Why do we also drop blank `avg_grade`? The next step averages it! ## Exercise 2 ::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"} 1. How many students left `sleep_hours` blank? Then count the blanks in **every** column. 2. Find students in Arts or Business who sleep less than 6 hours. Use `%in%`. 3. Find the same students again, this time using `|`. ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_filter'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_filter # Part 1: blanks in sleep_hours survey |> summarize() # Part 1b: blanks in every column # Hint: across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))) applies the count to every column survey |> summarize() # Part 2: Arts or Business, under 6 hours, with %in% survey |> filter() # Part 3: same students, using | survey |> filter() ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_filter' solution='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_filter #| solution: true # Part 1 survey |> summarize(n_missing = sum(is.na(sleep_hours))) # Part 1b survey |> summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) # Part 2 survey |> filter(program %in% c("Arts", "Business"), sleep_hours < 6) # Part 3 survey |> filter(program == "Arts" | program == "Business", sleep_hours < 6) ``` ::: # Step 3: group_by( ) and summarize( ) ::: {.notes} ~15 min for this section including Exercise 3. ::: ## Where we are in the pipeline ```{.r code-line-numbers="10-17"} sleep_summary <- survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program, sleep_group) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade), pct_passing = mean(avg_grade >= 60), any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50), .groups = "drop" ) ``` **Goal:** one row per program and sleep group, with a few summary numbers. ## Key Functions Here ::: {.callout-note title="`group_by()`"} Changes the unit of analysis by organizing rows into groups. It is invisible on its own, but changes how subsequent functions operate. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="`summarize()`"} Collapses multiple rows down into a single summary statistic per group. ::: ```r # Example: Calculate student counts and mean grades by program survey |> group_by(program) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ## Summaries of logical vectors In a numeric context, `TRUE` becomes **1** and `FALSE` becomes **0**. ::: {.callout-important title="Key idea"} - `sum(x)` gives the **number** of `TRUE`s - `mean(x)` gives the **proportion** of `TRUE`s (because `mean()` is just `sum()` divided by `length()`) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) ``` ::: ## `sum()` and `mean()` by program How many students in each program sleep under 6 hours, and what proportion is that? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> group_by(program) |> summarize( n_short = sum(sleep_hours < 6, na.rm = TRUE), prop_short = mean(sleep_hours < 6, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: ## Remember the `NA`s ::: {.callout-warning title="Without na.rm"} Try deleting `na.rm = TRUE` from the code above. One `NA` in a group makes the whole `sum()` or `mean()` `NA`. ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="na.rm changes the denominator"} `mean(x < 6, na.rm = TRUE)` is the proportion **among students who answered**. It does not count blank rows as `FALSE`. In our pipeline, we avoid the problem by filtering the blank rows out first. ::: ## `any()` and `all()` - `any(x)` is the equivalent of `|`: `TRUE` if there is at least one `TRUE` in `x` - `all(x)` is the equivalent of `&`: `TRUE` only if **every** value of `x` is `TRUE` - Like most summary functions, add `na.rm = TRUE` to drop missing values ::: {.cell} ```{webr} survey |> group_by(program) |> summarize( any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50, na.rm = TRUE), all_pass = all(avg_grade >= 50, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: - Often `any()` and `all()` are a bit too crude - We usually want to know *how many*, which is why `sum()` and `mean()` come first ## Putting it together ::: {.cell} ```{webr} sleep_summary <- survey |> mutate( sleep_group = case_when( sleep_hours < 6 ~ "Short", sleep_hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", sleep_hours > 7.5 ~ "Long" ) ) |> filter(!is.na(sleep_group), !is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program, sleep_group) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_grade = mean(avg_grade), pct_passing = mean(avg_grade >= 60), any_fail = any(avg_grade < 50), .groups = "drop" ) sleep_summary ``` ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Watch the group sizes"} Look at the `n` column. Some groups have only 10 to 15 students, so their averages are less trustworthy than the large ones. ::: ## Exercise 3 ::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"} For each **program**, find: - `n_short`: how many students sleep under 6 hours - `prop_short`: the proportion of students who sleep under 6 hours - `prop_early`: the proportion who have an early class (`has_early_class == "Yes"`) - `any_high`: whether any student has `avg_grade` of 95 or above ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_summarize'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_summarize survey |> filter(!is.na(sleep_hours),!is.na(has_early_class),!is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program) |> summarize( ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell exercise='ex_summarize' solution='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_summarize #| solution: true survey |> filter(!is.na(sleep_hours),!is.na(has_early_class),!is.na(avg_grade)) |> group_by(program) |> summarize( n_short = sum(sleep_hours < 6), prop_short = mean(sleep_hours < 6), prop_early = mean(has_early_class == "Yes"), any_high = any(avg_grade >= 95) ) ``` ::: # Wrap-up ::: {.notes} ~10 min. Then ~10 min of buffer, which you will probably need. ::: ## Back to the question {.smaller} > Do students who sleep less get lower grades, and does it depend on their program? - **Overall:** students who sleep more have higher average grades - **Within each program:** the differences are small and not consistent - **Why:** programs differ in both sleep and grades, so mixing them together created the overall pattern ::: {.callout-caution title="Caution: What we cannot say"} - This is survey data, so it shows **association**, not cause - Some groups are small, so differences of a point or two mean little - A good analyst checks the group sizes before telling a story ::: ## Chapter summary A logical vector is simple (each value is `TRUE`, `FALSE`, or `NA`), but it is very powerful. - **Create** them with `>`, `<`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, and `is.na()` - **Combine** them with `!`, `&`, and `|` - **Summarize** them with `any()`, `all()`, `sum()`, and `mean()` - **Transform** conditionally with `if_else()` and `case_when()` ## What's next Logical vectors will keep coming back: - In Chapter 14 (Strings), `str_detect(x, pattern)` returns a logical vector that is `TRUE` where elements of `x` match the `pattern` - In Chapter 17 (Dates and times), you will build logical vectors by comparing dates and times ::: {.callout-important title="Up Next"} **numbers and strings**. The survey has a `bedtime` column where students typed their bedtime in many different ways. We will clean it up. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
